item.title: Why did they ignore the cure?
item.description: Medical tradition blocked a life-saving discovery. Semmelweis identified hand disinfection as a way to cut puerperal fever. Peers rejected it because of cultural factors and a lack of theoretical framework, not because of his character. The evidence confirms that Semmelweis identified a life-saving practice that was initially rejected by the medical establishment due to a lack of theoretical framework and cultural resistance.

item.title: Who are you actually trusting with your future?
item.description: High active share is linked to outperformance. While many active funds underperform, those with the highest active share significantly outperform their benchmarks both before and after expenses. The evidence is mixed because results vary depending on the specific group of funds studied. The evidence is mixed, showing that while many active funds underperform, specific characteristics like high Active Share are linked to outperformance.

item.title: Which jobs will AI actually touch?
item.description: AI exposure varies from 9.4 to 81.7 percent. The impact of AI depends on your specific job category. Some roles show nearly total exposure, while others show very little. This evidence is mixed and based on preliminary studies. The evidence shows that AI impacts vary widely by occupation and may lead to complex human-AI collaborations rather than total automation.

item.title: Does your screen create a distorted mirror?
item.description: Online dating has specific psychological risks. The evidence shows that online dating is linked to negative impacts on body image and mental health. The evidence shows that online dating has specific psychological risks and that relationship outcomes are influenced by communication patterns rather than being simply similar to offline dating.

item.title: Does your screen actually help you remember?
item.description: Digital books can outperform paper with the right design. While paper generally shows a small to moderate advantage in comprehension, digital books with story-congruent enhancements can result in higher scores. This finding is currently considered emerging and the evidence is mixed. The evidence generally shows that reading on paper leads to slightly better comprehension than reading on a screen, though this effect varies significantly depending on the text genre, the reader's age, and the specific design of the digital medium.

item.title: Who sets the price you are willing to pay?
item.description: The first number you hear sets the price. Your brain uses a preceding number as a reference point to make judgments about what you are willing to pay. The evidence confirms that anchoring influences judgments and willingness to pay, though the effect size varies based on product type and measurement methodology.

item.title: What is circulating in your blood right now?
item.description: Microplastics are present in human blood. Studies have detected microplastics in the blood of humans. 88% of these particles are fragments and 79% are white or clear. The evidence confirms that microplastics are present in human blood and reproductive tissues, with some correlations to adverse pregnancy outcomes.

item.title: What is the cost of the extra hour?
item.description: Long hours increase your risk of stroke. Research shows that working long hours is linked to a higher risk of stroke and atrial fibrillation. This extends to broader occupational health issues. The evidence consistently links long working hours to increased risks of stroke, atrial fibrillation, and broader occupational health issues.

item.title: Does a like feel like a reward?
item.description: Likes activate the same brain circuitry as physical rewards. Providing likes to others triggers activity in the striatum and ventral tegmental area. This same circuitry processes reward. The evidence shows that 'likes' and popular content trigger reward-related brain activity and influence behavior, particularly in adolescents.

item.title: Does your phone drain your brain when you are not using it?
item.description: Your phone drains your brain even when it is silent. The mere presence of a smartphone reduces available cognitive capacity. This effect is most significant for those with high smartphone dependence. The evidence is mixed, with some studies showing reduced cognitive capacity and others finding no significant impact on performance.

item.title: You assume the universe is multiplying. The evidence shows it is stable.
item.description: Galaxy numbers do not increase tenfold. Evidence shows galaxy number densities remain relatively constant or reach equilibrium at specific redshifts. The evidence shows that galaxy number densities are relatively stable over certain redshift ranges and does not support the claim that there are ten times more galaxies than previously estimated.

item.title: Is there a limit to how long you can live?
item.description: The current human age limit will likely break. There is a greater than 99% probability that the current maximum reported age at death of 122 will be broken by 2100. The evidence is mixed. The evidence suggests that human lifespan is not currently capped at 122 and may be extendable through biological and pharmacological interventions.

item.title: Why do we choose people who are different?
item.description: Perceived similarity matters more than actual similarity. In existing relationships, how similar you think your partner is predicts attraction more than how similar you actually are. The evidence shows that while assortative mating leads to similarities in traits like education and height, the psychological attraction in long-term relationships depends more on how similar people perceive each other to be.

item.title: Why do you forgive people but punish machines?
item.description: You forgive a human but punish an algorithm. People use automated advice significantly less than human advice after receiving bad information. The evidence is mixed because the impact depends on how information is presented and on your personality traits. The evidence shows that while humans are more forgiving of errors than algorithms, the impact of showing those errors depends heavily on how the information is presented and the nature of the task.

item.title: You think the leftmost digit matters. The evidence is mixed.
item.description: Evidence on the. Some studies show neurological changes in the brain, while large-scale online experiments found no support for the left-digit effect. The evidence is mixed, with some studies showing neurological and cognitive effects of the left-digit while others find no significant impact on actual purchasing decisions.

item.title: Does your appearance dictate your career path?
item.description: Attractiveness is a variable weight in your success. While attractive people are often seen as more capable, the impact on service outcomes is inconsistent and can range from slightly negative to moderately positive. The evidence shows that physical attractiveness generally creates a positive bias in professional and leadership contexts, but the strength and direction of this effect vary significantly depending on the specific situation.

item.title: What if the story of 38 witnesses is a lie?
item.description: The killer was caught by two people who stepped in. The story of 38 silent witnesses is not supported by archival records. Two bystanders actually intervened to catch the killer. The evidence shows that the iconic narrative of 38 silent witnesses is not supported by archival records and contains significant factual errors.

item.title: Can a game actually make you smarter?
item.description: Your brain gets better at the game, not your life. Training produces improvements in specific skills like working memory, but these gains rarely transfer to general intelligence or real-world abilities. This evidence is mixed regarding the scale of these effects. The evidence shows that training produces 'near-transfer' improvements in the specific skills being practiced, but 'far-transfer' to general cognitive abilities is consistently small or non-existent.

item.title: Is your willpower actually your own?
item.description: Family background explains the marshmallow test. The link between waiting for a marshmallow and later success is largely a reflection of a child's early environment and social support., The evidence shows that while the marshmallow test correlates with certain outcomes, these links are significantly weakened or explained away by family background and social factors.

item.title: Does your screen provide connection or just a constant fear of being left out?
item.description: Online interactions can reduce loneliness. Specific types of online communication, such as one-to-one friendship and self-disclosure, can mitigate feelings of loneliness and stress. The evidence shows a strong association between FoMO and problematic smartphone use, but also highlights that specific positive online behaviors can have beneficial mental health outcomes.

item.title: Is sitting always the enemy of your health?
item.description: Moderate sitting may be protective for active people. While high sedentary time is linked to mortality, moderate sitting showed a protective effect in highly active individuals. The evidence on cognitive and long-term effects remains mixed. The evidence shows that while sedentary behavior is generally linked to higher mortality, the risk is complex and depends on the context of an individual's total activity levels.

item.title: Who is setting your internal pace?
item.description: Your cells have their own clocks. Circadian clocks exist in nearly every cell of your body, not just in your brain. The evidence confirms that circadian clocks are distributed throughout the body's tissues and can function independently of the central brain pacemaker.

item.title: Did you choose that option or did it choose you?
item.description: Pre-selected choices steer your behavior. When a choice is already made for you, you are more likely to select it. This is a documented effect of default nudges on human decision-making. The evidence confirms that defaults significantly influence decision-making, though their effectiveness varies depending on the domain, the perception of the choice, and cultural background.

item.title: Is your phone making you less present?
item.description: Phubbing harms relationships through exclusion and less intimacy. The damage to your connection with a partner is not primarily about conflict or jealousy. It is driven by feelings of exclusion and a lack of responsiveness. The evidence shows that partner phubbing consistently harms relationship quality, primarily through feelings of exclusion and reduced intimacy rather than just conflict.

item.title: Is dopamine about pleasure?
item.description: Dopamine signals reward prediction errors. Your brain calculates the difference between what you expected to get and what you actually received. The evidence shows that dopamine is a mechanism for calculating reward prediction errors and encoding subjective value to facilitate learning and reward-seeking behavior.

item.title: Who told the guards to be cruel?
item.description: The guards were told how to act. Experimenters gave the guards precise instructions on how to treat the prisoners and encouraged them to adopt tough roles. The evidence indicates that the Stanford Prison Experiment was heavily influenced by external instructions and prior student work rather than being a purely organic demonstration of role conformity.

item.title: Do violent video games change your behavior?
item.description: The evidence on violent video games is mixed. Some studies find negligible effects on aggression, while others find significant positive effects.,,,,, The research shows a lack of consensus, with results ranging from negligible to significant depending on the specific meta-analysis and methodology used.

item.title: You think experts have the edge. The data says otherwise.
item.description: AI narrows the gap between skilled and unskilled workers. Generative AI consistently boosts productivity and quality for lower-skilled or less experienced workers while reducing inequality. The evidence shows that generative AI consistently boosts productivity and quality for lower-skilled or less experienced workers while reducing inequality.

item.title: Why does your neighbor's salary matter to you?
item.description: Knowing you earn less can increase your effort. When workers see their peers earn more, they provide significantly more labor effort. This effect is often moderated by where you stand in your own company's hierarchy. The evidence shows that relative pay comparisons significantly impact subjective wellbeing and job satisfaction for those earning below the median, but these comparisons can also trigger increased labor effort or strategic business behaviors.

item.title: How much nature do you actually need?
item.description: Nature benefits peak at specific doses. While 120 minutes a week is linked to better health, the most effective interventions for mental health occur in doses of 20 to 90 minutes. The evidence shows that regular nature contact and structured nature-based interventions are linked to improved mental and physical health outcomes, with specific benefits observed for disadvantaged groups.

item.title: What are you missing right now?
item.description: You do not see what you are not looking for. Eighty-three percent of radiologists did not see a gorilla that was 48 times the size of the average nodule. They looked directly at its location. The evidence shows that inattentional blindness is a robust phenomenon where specific attentional goals and perceptual loads can cause people to miss highly salient, visible events.

item.title: Can you tell the difference between news and an ad?
item.description: You are likely being sold to right now. Fewer than 1 in 10 people can recognize native advertising. This means the vast majority of content you consume is actually paid promotion. The evidence shows that native advertising is frequently difficult to recognize, but the effectiveness of disclosures varies significantly depending on their design, position, and the user's prior experience.

item.title: Do trees really talk through fungi?
item.description: Trees may share resources but their importance is unclear. While common mycorrhizal networks can move zinc and water, their overall significance to the forest remains uncertain. The evidence is mixed. The evidence confirms that resource transfer occurs through these networks but highlights significant uncertainty regarding their ecological significance and potential drawbacks.

item.title: Does hearing a lie enough times make it true?
item.description: Repetition does not make opinions feel true. While repeated lies feel more factual, this effect does not apply to social-political opinions. Repetition increases perceived truthfulness for factual information by leveraging fluency, but this effect is limited by the type of content being presented.

item.title: How much of your behavior is a chemical reflex?
item.description: Lead exposure is linked to structural changes in the adult brain. Research shows childhood lead exposure is associated with region-specific reductions in adult gray matter volume in the prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate cortex. The evidence shows that lead exposure is associated with measurable cognitive deficits, structural brain volume reductions, and substantial economic impacts.

item.title: Why do you keep paying for things you don't use?
item.description: Inattention doubles seller revenues. Cancellation frictions driven by inattention or switching costs roughly double seller revenues on average. This finding is based on stylized models rather than a direct experimental trial. The evidence shows that while inattention creates significant profit for sellers, other factors like service complexity can negatively impact customer retention.

item.title: Can a machine hear your thoughts before you speak?
item.description: A brain implant decodes attempted speech into 78 words per minute. Cortical activity from a person with paralysis is translated into text or audio at various speeds. Systems range from 15.2 to 78 words per minute. The evidence shows that speech neuroprostheses can decode cortical activity into words and sentences for people with paralysis, with some systems reaching high accuracy and conversational speeds.

item.title: Is your behavior a choice or a reflex?
item.description: Complex behavior may not require complex cognition. While cephalopods possess large, complex brains, their behavioral flexibility could be driven by simpler mechanisms. The sources confirm that cephalopods have complex nervous systems and cognitive abilities, but they suggest that complex behavior might not always require complex cognition.

item.title: Who decides if you get the job?
item.description: Discrimination against the elderly and disabled is as severe as racial bias. Research shows that hiring discrimination against candidates with disabilities, older candidates, and less physically attractive candidates is as severe as treatment based on racial or ethnic characteristics. The evidence confirms that names and characteristics associated with race, age, and disability continue to result in fewer callbacks for many applicants.

item.title: Does your phone ruin your conversations?
item.description: The presence of a phone does not always hurt conversation quality. Research on whether a phone on a table ruins a conversation shows mixed results. It depends on the type of interaction and who is talking. The evidence is mixed, showing that while phone use (phubbing) consistently harms perceptions, the mere presence of a phone has inconsistent effects depending on the context and individual traits.
